l: Pleiades, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: The Pleiades were the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione: Alcyone, Merope, Celaeno, Electra, Sterope, Taygete, and Maia.

l: Alcyone, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Poseidon had intercourse with Alcyone, and she bore Aethusa, Hyrieus, and Hyperenor.

l: Merope, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Merope was married to Sisyphus.

l: Celaeno, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Poseidon had intercourse with Celaeno, and she bore Lycus, whom Poseidon made to dwell in the Islands of the Blest.

l: Maia, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Maia was the eldest of the daughters of Atlas and Pleione. She had Hermes by Zeus in a cave of Cyllene.

l: Poseidon, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Poseidon had Lycus by Celaeno and Aethusa, Hyrieus, and Hyperenor by Alcyone. He made Lycus dwell in the Islands of the Blest.

l: Apollo, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Apollo was herding the cattle that Hermes stole. He searched for them at Pylus, accused Hermes before Maia, brought Hermes to Zeus, and finally exchanged the cattle for the lyre.

l: Zeus, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Zeus fathered Hermes by Maia and fathered Zethus and Amphion by Antiope. He ordered Hermes to return Apollo's cattle and appointed Hermes as his herald and the herald of the infernal gods.

l: Hermes, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Hermes was born to Maia by Zeus in a cave of Cyllene. He stole Apollo's cattle, concealed and sacrificed some of them, made a lyre from a tortoise shell and cattle sinews, exchanged the lyre for the cattle, acquired Apollo's golden wand and the art of divination, and was appointed herald by Zeus.

l: Cyllene, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Cyllene was the place where the Pleiades were born and where Maia gave birth to Hermes in a cave. Hermes returned there after stealing Apollo's cattle, and Apollo went there to accuse him.

l: Pylus, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Hermes brought Apollo's cattle to Pylus, hid the rest in a cave, and sacrificed two of them. Apollo searched for the cattle at Pylus, questioned its inhabitants, and later received the cattle there from Hermes.

l: cave of Cyllene, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: The cave of Cyllene was where Maia gave birth to Hermes. Hermes was shown there by Maia after Apollo accused him.

l: cattle, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: The cattle were being herded by Apollo when Hermes stole them and took them to Pylus. Hermes hid some, sacrificed two, and later returned the cattle to Apollo in exchange for the lyre.

l: tortoise, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Hermes found a tortoise browsing before the cave at Cyllene. He cleaned out its shell and used it to make a lyre.

l: lyre, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Hermes made the lyre from a tortoise shell and cords made from the cattle he had sacrificed. Apollo exchanged the cattle for the lyre after hearing it.

l: golden wand, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Apollo offered Hermes the golden wand that he had possessed while herding cattle in exchange for Hermes's shepherd's pipe. Hermes also sought the art of divination.

l: shepherd's pipe, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: While herding the cattle, Hermes made a shepherd's pipe and played it. Apollo wanted it and offered his golden wand in exchange.

l: cattle theft by Hermes, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Hermes stole the cattle that Apollo was herding, taking them to Pylus and attempting to conceal the tracks. Apollo discovered through divination who had stolen them and accused Hermes.

l: exchange of the lyre for the cattle, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: After Hermes returned the cattle to Pylus, Apollo heard the lyre and gave the cattle to Hermes in exchange for it.

l: Hermes's appointment as herald, The Library, BOOK I[]].—continued
s: Zeus appointed Hermes as herald to himself and to the infernal gods.

l: The Library, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: The unit recounts that Apollo loved Coronis, who chose to live with Ischys, and that Apollo killed her while rescuing their child Aesculapius from the pyre. Aesculapius learned healing and hunting from Chiron and became skilled enough to prevent deaths and raise the dead. Zeus struck Aesculapius with a thunderbolt, after which Apollo slew the Cyclopes who had made it. Zeus ordered Apollo to serve Admetus for a year, and Apollo tended Admetus’s herds at Pherae.

l: Zeus, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Zeus feared that people might obtain the healing art from Aesculapius and help one another, so he struck Aesculapius with a thunderbolt. He intended to hurl Apollo into Tartarus for slaying the Cyclopes, but at Leto’s request ordered Apollo to serve Admetus for a year.

l: Apollo, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Apollo loved Coronis and had intercourse with her, and he later killed her after she chose to live with Ischys. He rescued their child Aesculapius from the burning pyre, slew the Cyclopes who had made Zeus’s thunderbolt, and served Admetus for a year at Zeus’s command.

l: Aesculapius, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Aesculapius was brought from Coronis’s pyre to Chiron, who raised him and taught him healing and hunting. He became a skilled surgeon, prevented some people from dying, and raised others from the dead by using blood from the Gorgon that he had received from Athena.

l: Coronis, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Coronis was loved by Apollo, but against her father’s judgment she preferred Ischys, brother of Caeneus, and lived with him. Apollo killed her, and while she was burning he rescued her child from the pyre.

l: Cyclopes, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: The Cyclopes had made the thunderbolt for Zeus. Apollo slew them after Zeus used the thunderbolt to strike Aesculapius.

l: Admetus, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Admetus received Apollo, who served him for a year at Pherae. Apollo tended Admetus’s herds and made all the female cattle give birth to twins.

l: thunderbolt, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: The thunderbolt was made by the Cyclopes for Zeus. Zeus used it to strike Aesculapius.

l: healing art, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Aesculapius learned the healing art from Chiron and practiced it extensively. Zeus feared that people might acquire the healing art from Aesculapius and use it to rescue one another.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Aesculapius raised some dead people by using blood from the Gorgon’s veins that he had received from Athena. The text names Capaneus, Lycurgus, Hippolytus, Tyndareus, Hymenaeus, and Glaucus as people reported to have been raised by him.

l: Coronis’s death, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Apollo killed Coronis after she chose to live with Ischys. As Coronis was burning, Apollo rescued her child from the pyre.

l: Apollo’s slaying of the Cyclopes, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: Apollo slew the Cyclopes because Zeus had struck Aesculapius with a thunderbolt. Zeus then intended to hurl Apollo into Tartarus, but ordered him instead to serve Admetus for a year.

l: Apollo’s servitude to Admetus, The Library, Taygete had by Zeus a son Lacedaemon, after
s: At Zeus’s command, Apollo served Admetus at Pherae for a year. He tended Admetus’s herds and made all the female cattle give birth to twins.

l: The Library, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: The unit recounts the genealogy and conflicts surrounding Tyndareus, Hippocoon, Icarius, and their descendants. Hippocoon expels Tyndareus and Icarius from Lacedaemon, but Heracles later kills Hippocoon and his sons, allowing Tyndareus to regain the kingdom. It describes the marriages and children of Tyndareus, Leda, Icarius, Penelope, Helen, and Menelaus, including the accounts of Helen’s birth from Leda or Nemesis. It also recounts Theseus’s abduction of Helen, her recovery by Castor and Pollux, and the oath taken by Helen’s suitors before Menelaus became her husband.

l: Tyndareus, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Tyndareus was a son of Oebalus and the nymph Batia, according to one genealogy. Hippocoon expelled him and Icarius from Lacedaemon, but after Heracles killed Hippocoon and his sons, Tyndareus returned and took the kingdom. He married Leda, chose Menelaus as Helen’s bridegroom, and caused Helen’s suitors to swear an oath.

l: Hippocoon, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Hippocoon was a son of Oebalus and the nymph Batia, according to one genealogy. With the help of his sons, he expelled Tyndareus and Icarius from Lacedaemon. Heracles later killed Hippocoon and his sons.

l: Icarius, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Icarius was expelled from Lacedaemon by Hippocoon together with Tyndareus. He later returned after Heracles killed Hippocoon and his sons. With Periboea, he had five sons and a daughter, Penelope, whom Odysseus married.

l: Hercules, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Heracles killed Hippocoon and his sons. After their deaths, Tyndareus and Icarius returned to Lacedaemon, and Tyndareus took the kingdom.

l: Leda, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Leda was the daughter of Thestius and the wife of Tyndareus. Zeus approached her in the form of a swan, and Tyndareus also cohabited with her on the same night. She bore Pollux and Helen to Zeus, and Castor and Clytaemnestra to Tyndareus.

l: Penelope, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Penelope was the daughter of Icarius and Periboea. Odysseus married her after Tyndareus helped arrange the marriage.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Odysseus was among the suitors of Helen. He promised to help Tyndareus arrange Penelope’s marriage if Tyndareus would assist him, and he proposed that all the suitors swear to defend the chosen bridegroom. Tyndareus then arranged for Odysseus to marry Penelope.

l: Clytaemnestra, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Clytaemnestra was a daughter of Tyndareus and Leda. Agamemnon married her, and she was also said to have been born from Tyndareus’s union with Leda.

l: Agamemnon, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Agamemnon was among the suitors of Helen. He married Clytaemnestra, the daughter of Tyndareus and Leda.

l: Zeus, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Zeus approached Leda in the form of a swan and fathered Pollux and Helen with her. In another account, Zeus pursued Nemesis, who changed into a goose, while Zeus changed into a swan; their union produced the egg from which Helen emerged.

l: Pollux, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Pollux was said to have been born to Zeus and Leda. He practiced boxing, and his bravery with Castor led both brothers to be called the Dioscuri. He and Castor recovered Helen from Aphidnae after Theseus carried her away.

l: Helen, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Helen was said to have been the daughter of Zeus and Leda, or, in another account, the daughter of Zeus and Nemesis. Theseus carried her to Aphidnae, but Pollux and Castor later captured the city and recovered her. Tyndareus chose Menelaus as her bridegroom, and she had Hermione and, according to some, Nicostratus by Menelaus.

l: Castor, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Castor was said to have been born to Tyndareus and Leda. He practiced warfare, while Pollux practiced boxing, and their bravery led both brothers to be called the Dioscuri. He and Pollux recovered Helen from Aphidnae after Theseus carried her away.

l: Theseus, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Theseus carried Helen away to Aphidnae when she had grown into a notably beautiful woman. While Theseus was in Hades, Castor and Pollux attacked Aphidnae, recovered Helen, and took Theseus’s mother Aethra captive.

l: Helen’s suitors, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Helen’s suitors included many kings and heroes, among them Odysseus, Diomedes, Antilochus, Agamemnon, Menelaus, Ajax, and others named in the unit. Tyndareus feared that choosing one suitor would cause the others to quarrel, so he had them swear to defend the chosen bridegroom.

l: Menelaus, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Menelaus was among Helen’s suitors and was chosen by Tyndareus as her bridegroom. With Helen he had a daughter, Hermione, and according to some accounts a son, Nicostratus.

l: Tyndareus's oath, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: The oath required all of Helen’s suitors to help the chosen bridegroom if another person wronged him concerning the marriage. Tyndareus imposed the oath after Odysseus proposed it as a way to prevent quarrels among the suitors.

l: marriage of Helen, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: Tyndareus chose Menelaus as Helen’s bridegroom after obtaining the oath of her suitors. The kings of Greece had gathered at Sparta to seek Helen’s hand.

l: Dioscuri, The Library, Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγοντες ᾿Αφαρέα μὲν καὶ Λεύκιππον
s: The Dioscuri were Castor and Pollux. They received this name because of their bravery, with Castor practicing warfare and Pollux practicing boxing.

l: The Library, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, were renowned for war and boxing and married the daughters of Leucippus after carrying them off from Messene. With Idas and Lynceus, the sons of Aphareus, they obtained cattle booty from Arcadia, but Idas seized the entire spoil after rapidly consuming his own and his brother’s shares. The Dioscuri attacked Messene to recover the cattle and other booty, leading to the deaths of Castor, Lynceus, and Idas and to Pollux’s ascent to heaven. Because Pollux refused immortality while Castor was dead, Zeus granted them alternating existence among the gods and mortals.

l: Castor, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Castor practised the art of war and, with Pollux, was called one of the Dioscuri. He carried off and married a daughter of Leucippus, had Anogon by Hilaira, and joined Pollux in taking cattle and other booty to Messene. Lynceus discovered Castor in hiding and revealed his position to Idas, who killed him.

l: Pollux, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Pollux practised boxing and, with Castor, was called one of the Dioscuri. He carried off and married a daughter of Leucippus and had Mnesileus by Phoebe. He killed Lynceus with a spear, was later taken up to heaven by Zeus, and refused to accept immortality while Castor was dead.

l: Dioscuri, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: The Dioscuri were Castor and Pollux, who were called so because of their manliness. They marched against Messene to recover cattle booty and other spoil, and after Castor’s death Zeus granted them alternating existence among the gods and mortals.

l: Messene, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: The daughters of Leucippus were carried off from Messene by Castor and Pollux, who married them. The Dioscuri later drove cattle and other booty to Messene and marched against it to recover the spoil.

l: sons of Aphareus, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: The sons of Aphareus were Idas and Lynceus. They joined Castor and Pollux in driving cattle booty from Arcadia, and later opposed the Dioscuri in the conflict over the spoil.

l: Idas, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Idas divided the cattle booty into four parts and declared that the first to eat his share would receive half the booty and the second the remainder. He consumed his own share and his brother’s before the others could act, then drove the cattle to Messene with Lynceus. After Lynceus revealed Castor’s position, Idas killed Castor; while being pursued by Pollux, he struck Pollux on the head with a stone, and Zeus killed Idas with a thunderbolt.

l: Lynceus, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Lynceus joined Idas, Castor, and Pollux in driving cattle booty from Arcadia. He spied Castor and revealed his position to Idas, who killed Castor. Pollux pursued Lynceus and killed him by throwing his spear, but Lynceus had wounded Pollux in the head with a stone.

l: cattle booty, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Cattle booty was driven from Arcadia by Castor, Pollux, Idas, and Lynceus. Idas divided it into four parts, consumed his own share and his brother’s, and drove the cattle to Messene; the Dioscuri later recovered that booty along with much other spoil.

l: Zeus, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: Zeus killed Idas with a thunderbolt and carried Pollux up to heaven. When Pollux refused immortality without Castor, Zeus allowed both of them to exist on alternating days among the gods and mortals.

l: alternation of divine and mortal existence, The Library, Of the sons born to Leda Castor practised the art
s: After Castor’s death, Pollux refused to accept immortality without his brother. Zeus therefore granted Castor and Pollux existence on alternating days among the gods and mortals.

l: The Library, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Electra, daughter of Atlas, had Iasion and Dardanus by Zeus. Iasion was killed by a thunderbolt after attempting to defile Demeter, while Dardanus left Samothrace, married Batia, and founded Dardania. Dardanus's descendants included Ilus, Erichthonius, Tros, Assaracus, Ganymede, Capys, Anchises, and Aeneas. Ilus founded Ilium in Phrygia after following a dappled cow and receiving the Palladium from Zeus.

l: Electra, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Electra, daughter of Atlas, had Iasion and Dardanus by Zeus.

l: Zeus, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Zeus was the father of Iasion and Dardanus with Electra. He killed Iasion with a thunderbolt after Iasion attempted to defile Demeter, and later showed Ilus the Palladium.

l: Iasion, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Iasion was the son of Electra and Zeus. He loved Demeter and was killed by a thunderbolt when he attempted to defile her.

l: Dardanus, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Dardanus was the son of Electra and Zeus and the brother of Iasion. Grieving over Iasion's death, he left Samothrace, came to the opposite mainland, married Batia, founded a city called Dardanus, and later called the whole country Dardania.

l: Samothrace, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Dardanus left Samothrace after the death of his brother Iasion and went to the opposite mainland.

l: Teucer, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Teucer, son of the river Scamander and the nymph Idaea, ruled the country to which Dardanus came. He welcomed Dardanus, gave him part of the land and Batia as a wife, and after Teucer died Dardanus called the whole country Dardania.

l: Batia, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Batia was the daughter of Teucer. She married Dardanus.

l: Dardania, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Dardania was the name Dardanus gave to the whole country after Teucer died.

l: Ilus, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Ilus was a son of Dardanus and became the founder of Ilium. He went to Phrygia, won a wrestling contest, followed a dappled cow as instructed, founded Ilium where it lay down, and received the Palladium after praying to Zeus.

l: Erichthonius, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Erichthonius was a son of Dardanus. He succeeded to the kingdom after Ilus died childless and had Tros by Astyoche, daughter of Simoeis.

l: Tros, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Tros was the son of Erichthonius and Astyoche. He succeeded to the kingdom, called the country Troy after himself, and had Cleopatra, Ilus, Assaracus, and Ganymede by Callirrhoe, daughter of Scamander.

l: Troy, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Troy was the name Tros gave to the country after himself.

l: Assaracus, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Assaracus was a son of Tros and Callirrhoe. With Hieromneme, daughter of Simoeis, he fathered Capys.

l: Ganymede, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Ganymede was a son of Tros and Callirrhoe. Because of his beauty, Zeus carried him away on an eagle and appointed him cupbearer of the gods in heaven.

l: Capys, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Capys was the son of Assaracus and Hieromneme. With Themiste, daughter of Ilus, he fathered Anchises.

l: Anchises, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Anchises was the son of Capys and Themiste. Aphrodite joined with him in love and bore him Aeneas and Lyrus.

l: Aphrodite, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Aphrodite joined with Anchises in love and bore him Aeneas and Lyrus.

l: Aeneas, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Aeneas was born to Anchises and Aphrodite.

l: Phrygia, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Ilus went to Phrygia and won a wrestling contest held by the king there. He then followed the dappled cow to the hill of the Phrygian Ate, where he founded Ilium.

l: dappled cow, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: The king gave Ilus a dappled cow and instructed him to found a city wherever it lay down. The cow lay down at the hill of the Phrygian Ate, and Ilus founded Ilium there.

l: Ilium, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: Ilus founded Ilium at the place where the dappled cow lay down. After praying to Zeus, Ilus saw the Palladium lying before his tent.

l: Palladium, The Library, XII. Ἠλέκτρας δὲ τῆς "Ἄτλαντος καὶ Διὸς
s: The Palladium fell from heaven and appeared before Ilus's tent after he prayed to Zeus. It was three cubits high, had joined feet, held an upright spear in its right hand, and held a distaff and spindle in the other.

l: The Library, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: The unit recounts the origin and fate of the Palladium, an image made by Athena for Pallas and later thrown by Zeus into the land of Ilium, where Ilus built it a temple. It then traces the lineage of Laomedon, including Podarces, who became Priam after Ilium was captured by Heracles. Priam’s son Aesacus interpreted Hecuba’s dream of a firebrand as a prophecy that her unborn child would destroy the city and advised exposing the infant. The exposed child, Paris, was nursed by a bear, raised by Agelaus, and later called Alexander for defending flocks and repelling robbers.

l: Palladium, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: The Palladium was a wooden image made by Athena in the likeness of Pallas, with the aegis placed around its breast. Zeus later threw it with Ate into the land of Ilium, where Ilus built a temple for it and honored it.

l: Athena, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Athena was raised by Triton and practiced the arts of war with Pallas. She wounded Pallas during a quarrel, then made a wooden image in Pallas’s likeness, placed the aegis around it, and honored it beside Zeus.

l: Pallas, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Pallas was Triton’s daughter and practiced the arts of war with Athena. When she was about to strike Athena, Zeus interposed the aegis; startled, Pallas looked up and was wounded by Athena.

l: Zeus, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Zeus interposed the aegis when Pallas was about to strike Athena. He later threw the Palladium with Ate into the land of Ilium.

l: Podarces, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Podarces was one of Laomedon’s sons. After Ilium was captured by Heracles, Podarces came to the throne and was called Priam.

l: Priam, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Priam was Podarces, who became king after Ilium was captured by Heracles. He first married Arisbe and later married Hecuba; after learning of Hecuba’s dream, he summoned Aesacus and followed the advice to expose the newborn child.

l: Ilium, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Ilium received the Palladium after Zeus threw it into its land, and Ilus built a temple for the image. Ilium was later captured by Heracles.

l: Aesacus, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Aesacus was the son of Priam and Arisbe and had learned dream interpretation from his maternal grandfather, Merops. After Priam summoned him to interpret Hecuba’s dream, Aesacus declared that the child would bring ruin to the country and advised that the infant be exposed.

l: Hecuba, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Hecuba was Priam’s second wife. Before giving birth to another child, she dreamed that she had brought forth a fiery firebrand whose flames spread through and burned the whole city.

l: Paris, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Paris was the infant born after Hecuba’s dream of the firebrand. Priam ordered him exposed on Ida, but a bear nursed him for five days; Agelaus then found him alive, took him away, and raised him as his own son.

l: Alexander, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Alexander was the name later given to Paris when he became a young man who excelled in beauty and strength. He received the name because he repelled robbers and defended the flocks.

l: Hecuba's dream of the firebrand, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: Hecuba’s dream showed her giving birth to a fiery firebrand that spread through the entire city and burned it. Aesacus interpreted the dream as meaning that the child would bring ruin to the country.

l: infant Paris, The Library, Ἱστορία δὲ! ἡ περὶ τοῦ παλλαδίου τοιάδε
s: The infant Paris was regarded as a danger to the country because of Hecuba’s dream. Priam gave him to a servant named Agelaus to expose on Ida, but a bear nursed him for five days, after which Agelaus found him alive and raised him as his own child.

l: The Library, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Hecuba bears daughters and sons, including Cassandra and Troilus, while Priam has many other sons and daughters by other women. Apollo offers to teach Cassandra prophecy, but after she refuses his advances, he removes its power to persuade. Hector marries Andromache, while Alexander marries Oenone before abducting Helen from Sparta; during the Trojan War, Alexander is wounded by Philoctetes, returns to Oenone, and dies after she refuses to treat him. Asopus is described through several accounts of his parentage, and Zeus abducts his daughter Aegina.

l: Hecuba, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Hecuba gives birth to daughters including Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena, and Cassandra. She later bears Deiphobus, Helenus, Pammon, Polites, Antiphus, Hipponous, Polydorus, and Troilus; Troilus is said to have been fathered by Apollo.

l: Cassandra, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Apollo promises to teach Cassandra prophecy in exchange for her favours. After she learns prophecy but refuses his advances, Apollo deprives her prophecies of the power to persuade.

l: Apollo, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Apollo promises to teach Cassandra prophecy in order to gain her favours. When she refuses him after learning the art, he removes her prophecy's power to persuade; Troilus is also said to have been born to Hecuba by Apollo.

l: prophecy, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Cassandra learns prophecy from Apollo, but Apollo deprives it of the power to persuade after she refuses his favours.

l: Priam, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Priam has many sons by other women, including Melanippus, Gorgythion, Philaemon, Hippothous, Glaucus, Agathon, Chersidamas, Evagoras, Hippodamas, Mestor, Atas, Doryclus, Lycaon, Dryops, Bias, Chromius, Astygonus, Telestas, Evander, Cebriones, Mylius, Archemachus, Laodocus, Echephron, Idomeneus, Hyperion, Ascanius, Democoon, Aretus, Deiopites, Clonius, Echemmon, Hypirochus, Aegeoneus, Lysithous, and Polymedon. His daughters by other women are Medusa, Medesicaste, Lysimache, and Aristodeme.

l: Andromache, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Andromache, the daughter of Eetion, marries Hector.

l: Alexander, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Alexander marries Oenone, the daughter of the river Cebrenus. He abducts Helen from Sparta, is later wounded by Philoctetes during the war against Troy, and returns to Oenone, who refuses to treat him; he dies while being carried back to Troy.

l: Oenone, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Oenone, the daughter of Cebrenus, learns prophecy from Rhea and warns Alexander not to sail for Helen. She says that only she can heal him if he is wounded, but when he returns wounded, she refuses treatment out of resentment; after changing her mind and bringing medicines, she finds Alexander dead and hangs herself.

l: Helen, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Alexander abducts Helen from Sparta.

l: Sparta, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Alexander abducts Helen from Sparta.

l: Troy, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Troy is at war when Alexander is wounded by Philoctetes with Heracles' bows. Alexander dies while being carried back to Troy.

l: Asopus, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Asopus is identified as a river whose parentage is variously given: he is the son of Oceanus and Tethys, or, according to Acusilaus, of Poseidon and Pero, or, according to others, of Zeus and Eurynome. He marries Metope, who bears him Ismenus, Pelasgus, and twenty daughters.

l: Zeus, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Zeus abducts Aegina, one of the daughters of Asopus and Metope.

l: Aegina, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Aegina is one of the twenty daughters born to Asopus and Metope. Zeus abducts her.

l: Alexander’s voyage to Helen, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: Oenone warns Alexander not to sail for Helen. He does not heed her and abducts Helen from Sparta.

l: Trojan War, The Library, - After him Hecuba gave birth to daughters, Creusa,
s: During the war against Troy, Alexander is wounded by Philoctetes with Heracles' bows. He returns to Oenone for treatment but dies after she initially refuses to heal him.

l: The Library, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Alexander is wounded by Philoctetes, returns to Oenone for healing, and dies after she initially refuses to help him; Oenone then kills herself. Asopus searches for Aegina after Zeus carries her away, and Zeus fathers Aeacus with her on the island later called Aegina. Aeacus fathers Peleus, Telamon, and Phocus, but Peleus and Telamon kill Phocus and are driven into exile. Telamon receives the kingship of Salamis from Cychreus and later fathers Ajax, while Peleus goes to Phthia.

l: Alexander, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Alexander married Oenone and carried Helen from Sparta to Troy. After Philoctetes wounded him with the bow of Hercules, he returned to Oenone, who refused to heal him; he was carried to Troy and died.

l: Oenone, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Oenone, daughter of the river Cebren, had learned prophecy from Rhea and warned Alexander not to sail for Helen. She refused to heal Alexander when he returned wounded, but later repented; finding him dead, she hanged herself.

l: Troy, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Troy was besieged after Alexander carried Helen away from Sparta. Alexander was carried back to Troy after Oenone refused to heal him and died there.

l: Asopus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Asopus was said to be a son of Ocean and Tethys, of Pero and Poseidon, or of Zeus and Eurynome. He married Metope and fathered Ismenus, Pelagon, and twenty daughters, including Aegina; he pursued Zeus to Corinth after Zeus carried Aegina away, but Zeus drove him back to his own streams with thunderbolts.

l: Poseidon, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Poseidon was named in two genealogies: Asopus was said to be the son of Pero and Poseidon, and Cychreus was said to be the son of Poseidon and Salamis.

l: Zeus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Zeus carried Aegina away and, after Asopus learned from Sisyphus who the ravisher was, drove Asopus back to his own streams with thunderbolts. He took Aegina to the island then called Oenone and fathered Aeacus with her, and later made ants into men for Aeacus.

l: Aegina, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Aegina was one of Asopus and Metope's daughters. Zeus carried her away to the island then called Oenone, where he fathered Aeacus with her.

l: Aegina (island), The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: The island was formerly called Oenone and was later called Aegina after Aegina. Zeus and Aegina had Aeacus there, and Zeus made the ants of the island into men for Aeacus.

l: Aeacus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Aeacus was the son of Zeus and Aegina and became the father of Peleus, Telamon, and Phocus. He was described as the most pious of men, prayed for Greece during its infertility, and drove Peleus and Telamon from Aegina after the murder of Phocus. After his death, he was honored in the abode of Pluto and guarded the keys of Hades.

l: Peleus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Peleus was a son of Aeacus and Endeis and a brother of Telamon. He and Telamon plotted against Phocus, hid his body after his death, and were driven from Aegina; Peleus later went to Phthia.

l: Telamon, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Telamon was described either as a son of Aeacus and Endeis or, by Pherecydes, as a son of Actaeus and Glauce. He killed Phocus by throwing a quoit at his head, was driven from Aegina, received the kingship of Salamis from Cychreus, and later fathered Ajax with Periboea and Teucer with Hesione.

l: Cychreus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Cychreus was the son of Poseidon and Salamis, daughter of Asopus. He became king of Salamis after killing a snake that ravaged the island, and because he died childless he gave the kingdom to Telamon.

l: Phocus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Phocus was the son of Aeacus and Psamathe, who turned herself into a seal to avoid Aeacus's embraces. Because Phocus excelled in athletic contests, Peleus and Telamon plotted against him, and Telamon killed him with a quoit.

l: Greece, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Greece suffered infertility because Pelops had killed Stymphalus, king of the Arcadians, and scattered his limbs. Oracles declared that Greece would be freed from its troubles if Aeacus prayed on its behalf, and the infertility ended after he did so.

l: Pelops, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Pelops caused Greece to suffer infertility after he killed Stymphalus, king of the Arcadians, while pretending friendship and scattered his limbs.

l: murder of Phocus, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: The murder of Phocus was committed by Telamon, with Peleus helping to carry and hide the body. After the murder was discovered, Aeacus drove Peleus and Telamon from Aegina.

l: Salamis, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Salamis was ruled by Cychreus, who had become king after killing a snake that ravaged the island. When Cychreus died childless, he gave the kingdom to Telamon.

l: Ajax, The Library, Now Hector married Andromache, daughter of
s: Ajax was the son of Telamon and Periboea, daughter of Alcathus. Telamon gave him the name Ajax after an eagle appeared following Hercules's prayer for a male child.

l: The Library, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Peleus is purified by Acastus after accidentally killing Eurytion during the Calydonian boar hunt, but Acastus’s wife Astydamia falsely accuses him and Acastus abandons him on Pelion. Chiron saves Peleus and restores his hidden sword. Peleus marries Thetis after overcoming her transformations, and the gods celebrate their marriage, but Thetis leaves after Peleus interrupts her attempt to make their child immortal. Chiron raises the child, names him Achilles, and later Peleus joins Jason and the Dioscuri in sacking Iolcus and killing Astydamia.

l: Peleus, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Peleus was purified by Eurytion after fleeing to Phthia, received Eurytion’s daughter Antigone and a third of the country, and had a daughter Polydora. During the Calydonian boar hunt he accidentally killed Eurytion, fled again to Iolcus, and was purified by Acastus. At the games for Pelias he wrestled with Atalanta. After Astydamia falsely accused him, Acastus took him hunting on Pelion, abandoned him, and hid his sword, but Chiron saved him and returned it. Peleus later married Polydora and then Thetis, received an ashen spear from Chiron and immortal horses from Poseidon, and brought his child to Chiron after Thetis left. He later joined Jason and the Dioscuri in sacking Iolcus and killed Astydamia.

l: Acastus, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Acastus purified Peleus at Iolcus after Peleus fled from Phthia. After Astydamia accused Peleus of attempting her virtue, Acastus took Peleus hunting on Pelion rather than killing the man he had purified, abandoned him while he slept, and hid his sword in cows’ dung.

l: Astydamia, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Astydamia, the wife of Acastus, fell in love with Peleus and proposed a meeting to him. When he refused, she falsely told her husband that Peleus had attempted her virtue; after Peleus later returned with Jason and the Dioscuri, he killed her and had her body cut apart so that his army could pass through Iolcus.

l: Pelion, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Pelion was the place where Acastus took Peleus for a hunt and later abandoned him asleep. Peleus was threatened by centaurs there, but Chiron rescued him and found and returned his sword.

l: Chiron, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Chiron advised Peleus to seize and hold Thetis despite her transformations. He saved Peleus from the centaurs on Pelion, found and returned Peleus’s sword, gave Peleus an ashen spear, and later received and raised Peleus’s child, feeding him the entrails of lions and wild swine and the marrow of bears.

l: Thetis, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Thetis, daughter of Nereus, was sought in marriage by Zeus and Poseidon until a prophecy declared that her son would be mightier than his father. She transformed into fire, water, and a beast while Peleus tried to seize her, but he held her until she resumed her original form. After marrying Peleus, she secretly tried to make their child immortal by placing him in fire at night and anointing him with ambrosia by day; when Peleus interrupted her, she left the infant and returned to the Nereids.

l: The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: The marriage of Peleus and Thetis took place on Pelion, where the gods celebrated it with a feast and song. Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear, and Poseidon gave him the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus.

l: Achilles, The Library, XIII. Peleus fled to Phthia to the court of Eurytion,
s: Achilles was the child of Peleus and Thetis. After Thetis left him, Chiron raised him on the entrails of lions and wild swine and the marrow of bears; Chiron named him Achilles because he had not put his lips to the breast, although his earlier name was Ligyron.

l: The Library, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: The unit concerns Achilles’s concealment at Lycomedes’s court and his eventual departure for Troy. Thetis disguises Achilles as a girl because Calchas has declared that Troy cannot be taken without him, while fearing that he will die if he campaigns. Achilles has a son, Pyrrhus, with Deidamia, and Odysseus discovers him by sounding a trumpet. Achilles travels to Troy with Phoenix and Patroclus, whose earlier history is also recounted.

l: Achilles, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: When he was nine years old, Achilles was said to be necessary for the capture of Troy. Thetis disguised him in female clothing and entrusted him to Lycomedes as a maiden; while there, he had a son with Deidamia. Odysseus discovered him by sounding a trumpet, after which Achilles went to Troy accompanied by Phoenix and Patroclus.

l: Troy, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Calchas declared that Troy could not be taken without Achilles. Achilles later went there after Odysseus discovered him at Lycomedes’s court.

l: Thetis, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Thetis foresaw that Achilles would die if he went to war. She therefore disguised him in female clothing and placed him with Lycomedes as a maiden.

l: Lycomedes, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Lycomedes received Achilles from Thetis and kept him at his court disguised as a maiden. His daughter Deidamia had a son by Achilles there.

l: Deidamia, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Deidamia, daughter of Lycomedes, had a son named Pyrrhus by Achilles while he was being brought up at her father’s court.

l: Ulysses, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Odysseus searched for Achilles after learning that he was at Lycomedes’s court. He found him by using the sound of a trumpet, and Achilles then went to Troy.

l: war against Troy, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Calchas declared that Troy could not be captured without Achilles. Thetis foresaw that Achilles would die if he went campaigning.

l: Phoenix, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Phoenix, son of Amyntor, accompanied Achilles to Troy. His father had blinded him after a concubine falsely accused him of seduction; Peleus brought him to Chiron, who restored his sight, and Peleus then made him king of the Dolopians.

l: Peleus, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Peleus brought the blinded Phoenix to Chiron for healing. After Chiron restored Phoenix’s sight, Peleus made him king of the Dolopians. Peleus also gave refuge to Patroclus after Patroclus fled from Opus.

l: Chiron, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Chiron treated Phoenix after Phoenix had been blinded by his father and restored his sight.

l: Patroclus, The Library, Os δὲ ἐγένετο ἐνναετὴς ᾿Αχιλλεύς, Κάλχαντος
s: Patroclus, son of Menoetius, accompanied Achilles. At Opus he killed Cleitonymus, son of Amphidamas, during a quarrel in a game of knucklebones, then fled with his father to Peleus and lived there; he became Achilles’s beloved.

l: The Library, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Cecrops, an autochthonous king with the body of a man and a serpent, was the first king of Attica and renamed the country Cecropia. Poseidon and Athena contested possession of Attica, but the twelve gods awarded it to Athena after Cecrops testified that she had first planted the olive-tree. Athena named the city Athens, while Poseidon flooded the Thriasian plain in anger. The unit also traces Cinyras’s lineage and reports that Adonis was killed by a boar while hunting.

l: Cecrops, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Cecrops was autochthonous and had a body compounded of a man and a serpent. He was the first king of Attica, renamed the country Cecropia after himself, and testified that Athena had been the first to plant the olive-tree.

l: Attica, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Attica was formerly called Acte and was renamed Cecropia by Cecrops. Poseidon and Athena contested possession of it, and the twelve gods awarded it to Athena; Poseidon then flooded the Thriasian plain and laid Attica under the sea.

l: Poseidon, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Poseidon came first to Attica and struck the middle of the acropolis with his trident, producing the sea called Erechtheis. He contested Attica with Athena, lost when the twelve gods judged in her favor, and flooded the Thriasian plain in anger.

l: Athena, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Athena came to Attica after Poseidon and planted the olive-tree, calling Cecrops to witness her act. The twelve gods awarded Attica to her, and she named the city Athens after herself.

l: the olive-tree, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: The olive-tree was planted by Athena in Attica and was shown in the Pandrosium. Its planting served as evidence in the contest between Athena and Poseidon.

l: the contest for Attica, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: The contest for Attica was between Poseidon and Athena. Zeus appointed the twelve gods as judges, and they awarded the country to Athena because Cecrops testified that she had first planted the olive-tree.

l: Athens, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Athena named the city Athens after herself after the twelve gods awarded her possession of Attica.

l: Cinyras, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Cinyras was the son of Sandocus and Pharnace. After coming to Cyprus with his people, he founded Paphos, where he married Metharme and fathered Oxyporus, Adonis, Orsedice, Laogore, and Braesia.

l: Adonis, The Library, XIV. Κέκροψ αὐτόχθων, συμφυὲς ἔχων σῶμα
s: Adonis was a son of Cinyras and Metharme according to this account. While still a boy, he was wounded and killed by a boar while hunting because of the anger of Artemis.

l: The Library, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: The unit concerns Smyrna, daughter of Thias, king of Assyria, and her illicit passion for her father. With her nurse's help, Smyrna shares her father's bed for twelve nights, is pursued when he discovers this, and is transformed by the gods into a myrrh tree. Adonis is born from the tree, and Aphrodite and Persephone dispute possession of him until Zeus divides the year among Adonis, Persephone, and Aphrodite. Adonis later dies after being struck by a boar while hunting.

l: Thias, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Thias is identified as king of Assyria and the father of Smyrna. He unknowingly shares his bed with Smyrna for twelve nights, then pursues her with a sword after discovering what happened.

l: Smyrna, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Smyrna is the daughter of Thias. Because of Aphrodite's anger, she conceives a passion for her father, shares his bed for twelve nights with her nurse's help, is pursued by him, and is transformed into a myrrh tree by the gods.

l: Aphrodite, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Aphrodite is angered because Smyrna does not honour her, and Smyrna consequently conceives a passion for her father. Aphrodite hides the infant Adonis in a chest and entrusts him to Persephone, later receiving one part of his year.

l: theoi, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: The gods pity Smyrna after she prays to become invisible and transform her into the tree called smyrna, or myrrh.

l: the myrrh tree, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: The myrrh tree is the form into which Smyrna is transformed. Ten months later, it splits open and Adonis is born from it.

l: Adonis, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Adonis is born from the myrrh tree ten months after Smyrna's transformation. Aphrodite hides him as an infant, and Zeus assigns him portions of the year with himself, Persephone, and Aphrodite; later, Adonis dies after being struck by a boar while hunting.

l: Persephone, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Persephone receives the infant Adonis from Aphrodite but refuses to give him back after seeing him. Zeus assigns Adonis one part of the year to remain with Persephone.

l: Zeus, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.
s: Zeus presides over the judgment concerning Adonis and divides the year into three parts. He assigns one part to Adonis by himself, one with Persephone, and one with Aphrodite.

l: Aphrodite and Persephone's dispute over Adonis, The Library, βασιλέως ᾿Ασσυρίων, ὃ ὃς ἔσχε θυγατέρα Σμύρναν.

s: Zeus divides the year into three parts for Adonis: one part by himself, one part with Persephone, and one part with Aphrodite.

s: When Smyrna is pursued by her father after he discovers the intercourse, she prays to the gods to become invisible. The gods pity her and transform her into a myrrh tree.

s: Because of Adonis's beauty, Aphrodite hides him as an infant in a chest, unknown to the gods, and entrusts him to Persephone.

Amphictyon expels Cranaus and rules for twelve years before Erichthonius expels him. Erichthonius is said either to be the son of Hephaestus and Atthis or of Hephaestus and Athena, with the latter account involving Athena's visit to Hephaestus for weapons.

l: Cecrops, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Cecrops dies, after which Cranaus becomes king.

l: Cranaus, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Cranaus becomes king after Cecrops and is described as autochthonous. He marries Pedias and has Cranaus, Cranaichme, and Atthis; after Atthis dies as a virgin, he names the country Atthis. Amphictyon later expels him.

l: Deucalion, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Deucalion's flood is said to occur during the reign of Cranaus. Some say Amphictyon is Deucalion's son.

l: Deucalion’s flood, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: The flood of Deucalion is said to occur during Cranaus's reign.

l: Atthis, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Atthis is a daughter of Cranaus. She dies while still a virgin, and Cranaus names the country Atthis after her. In one account, she is the mother of Erichthonius with Hephaestus.

l: Amphictyon, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Amphictyon expels Cranaus and becomes king. He rules for twelve years before Erichthonius expels him; some say he is the son of Deucalion, while others call him autochthonous.

l: Erichthonius, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Erichthonius expels Amphictyon after Amphictyon has ruled for twelve years. He is said either to be the son of Hephaestus and Atthis or of Hephaestus and Athena.

l: Hephaestus, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Hephaestus is named as the father of Erichthonius in both accounts: with Atthis in one account and with Athena in another. In the account involving Athena, she comes to him because she wants weapons to be made.

l: Athena, The Library, Κέκροπος δὲ ἀποθανόντος Κραναὸς «ἐβασί-
s: Athena is named as the mother of Erichthonius in one account. She comes to Hephaestus because she wants weapons to be made, and he falls into desire for her after being abandoned by Aphrodite.

s: After Cecrops died, Cranaus became king of Athens, but Amphictyon expelled him and later Erichthonius expelled Amphictyon. Erichthonius was associated with Athena and Hephaestus, was raised by Athena, became king of Athens, established the Panathenaea, and married Praxithea, whose son was Pandion. During Pandion’s reign, Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica; Dionysus taught Icarius wine-making, but shepherds killed Icarius after drinking the undiluted wine. Icarius’s daughter Erigone found his body with the help of her dog Maera and hanged herself.

l: Cecrops, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne. Pandrosus, to whom Athena entrusted Erichthonius, was a daughter of Cecrops.

l: Cranaus, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Cranaus succeeded Cecrops as king and was described as a son of the soil. He married Pedias and had Cranae, Menaechme, and Atthis; after Atthis died unmarried, he called the country Atthis. Amphictyon later expelled him.

l: Amphictyon, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Amphictyon expelled Cranaus and ruled in his place. He was said either to be a son of Deucalion or a son of the soil, and after twelve years Erichthonius expelled him.

l: Erichthonius, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Erichthonius was variously said to be the son of Hephaestus and Atthis, or of Hephaestus and Athena. Athena raised him, and he later expelled Amphictyon, became king of Athens, established the Panathenaea, and married Praxithea, with whom he had Pandion.

l: Athena, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Athena was pursued by Hephaestus, whose seed fell on her leg and was wiped off with wool and thrown onto the ground, where Erichthonius was produced. She secretly raised Erichthonius, placed him in a chest, and entrusted him to Pandrosus, forbidding the chest to be opened. She later raised Erichthonius in her precinct, and he established her wooden image on the acropolis.

l: Pandrosus, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Athena entrusted the chest containing Erichthonius to Pandrosus, daughter of Cecrops, and forbade her to open it. Pandrosus’s sisters opened it out of curiosity and saw the infant with a serpent.

l: Pandion, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Pandion became king after Erichthonius died and was buried in Athena’s precinct. During his reign Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica.

l: Demeter, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Demeter came to Attica during the reign of Pandion and was welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis.

l: Dionysus, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Dionysus came to Attica during the reign of Pandion and was received by Icarius. He gave Icarius a vine branch and taught him about wine-making.

l: Icarius, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Icarius received a vine branch from Dionysus and learned wine-making. He gave the drink to shepherds, who, believing themselves bewitched after drinking it undiluted, killed him; his dog Maera later helped Erigone find his body.

l: Erigone, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Erigone searched for her father Icarius after his death. Guided by Maera to his body, she mourned him and hanged herself.

l: birth of Erichthonius, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: When Athena fled from Hephaestus, his seed fell on her leg, and she wiped it off with wool and threw it onto the ground. As Athena fled and the seed fell to the ground, Erichthonius was produced.

l: Acropolis of Athens, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: The sisters of Pandrosus opened the chest containing Erichthonius and, after seeing the infant with a serpent, were either destroyed by the serpent or driven mad and threw themselves down from the acropolis. Erichthonius later set up the wooden image of Athena on the acropolis.

l: Athens, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Erichthonius expelled Amphictyon and became king of Athens. He established the Panathenaea and set up the wooden image of Athena on the acropolis.

l: chest containing Erichthonius, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Athena placed Erichthonius in a chest and entrusted it to Pandrosus, forbidding the chest to be opened. Pandrosus’s sisters nevertheless opened it out of curiosity and saw the infant with a serpent.

l: serpent guarding Erichthonius, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: A serpent was seen coiled around the infant Erichthonius when the sisters of Pandrosus opened his chest. According to one account it destroyed them; according to another, Athena’s anger drove them mad and caused them to throw themselves from the acropolis.

l: Panathenaea, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Erichthonius instituted the festival of the Panathenaea after becoming king of Athens.

l: arrival of Demeter and Dionysus in Attica, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica during the reign of Pandion. Demeter was welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis, while Dionysus was received by Icarius.

l: Attica, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Demeter and Dionysus came to Attica during the reign of Pandion. Dionysus taught Icarius wine-making there.

l: Eleusis, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Demeter was welcomed by Celeus at Eleusis when she came to Attica.

l: wine-making, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Dionysus gave Icarius a vine branch and taught him about wine-making. Icarius then gave the resulting drink to shepherds.

l: Icarius’s killing, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: Shepherds tasted the drink given to them by Icarius and drank it copiously without water. Believing themselves bewitched, they killed Icarius, though by day they understood what had happened and buried him.

l: Erigone’s suicide, The Library, When Cecrops died, Cranaus came to the throne?!;
s: After Maera led Erigone to the buried body of Icarius, Erigone mourned her father and hanged herself.

s: Pandion married Zeuxippe and had Procne, Philomela, Erechtheus, and Butes. During a war with Labdacus, Pandion called on Tereus, who helped him win and then married Procne; they had a son, Itys. Tereus violated Philomela, cut out her tongue, and concealed her, but she communicated her suffering to Procne by weaving letters into a garment. Procne killed Itys and served him to Tereus, after which Procne became a nightingale, Philomela a swallow, and Tereus a hoopoe.

l: Pandion, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother's sister, and had Procne, Philomela, Erechtheus, and Butes. When war broke out with Labdacus over boundaries, he called on Tereus for help and, after the victory, gave Procne to Tereus in marriage.

l: Procne, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Procne married Tereus and had a son, Itys. After learning of Philomela's suffering, she killed Itys and served him to Tereus; while fleeing with Philomela, she was transformed into a nightingale.

l: Philomela, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Philomela was violated by Tereus after he told her that Procne was dead, and he cut out her tongue. She communicated her suffering to Procne by weaving letters into a garment, then fled with her and was transformed into a swallow.

l: Tereus, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Tereus, identified as the son of Ares and associated with Thrace, helped Pandion defeat Labdacus and married Procne, with whom he had Itys. He violated Philomela, cut out her tongue, and concealed her; after Procne served him Itys, he pursued the sisters with an axe and was transformed into a hoopoe.

l: Itys, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Itys was the son of Tereus and Procne. Procne killed him, cooked him, and served him to Tereus without his knowledge.

l: Daulia, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: Daulia in Phocis is identified as the place where Procne, Philomela, and Tereus were overtaken during the pursuit and transformed.

l: nightingale, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: The nightingale is the transformed form of Procne. It continued to utter the cry associated with the moment of transformation and was said to flee while plaintively calling the name of her dead son, Itys.

l: Hoopoe, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: The hoopoe is the transformed form of Tereus. It continued to pursue his cruel wife after the transformation.

l: swallow, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: The swallow is the transformed form of Philomela.

l: transformation into birds, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: In Daulia of Phocis, Procne, Philomela, and Tereus prayed to the gods to become birds while Tereus pursued the two sisters. Procne became a nightingale, Philomela a swallow, and Tereus a hoopoe.

l: Itys's murder, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: After learning of Philomela's suffering, Procne killed Itys, cooked him, and served him to Tereus, who was unaware that the meal was his son's body.

l: Philomela's mutilation, The Library, Pandion married Zeuxippe, his mother’s sister,!
s: After violating Philomela and telling her that Procne was dead, Tereus cut out her tongue and concealed her. Philomela then conveyed her suffering to Procne by weaving letters into a garment.

l: The Library, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: The unit describes the descendants of Pandion, including Erechtheus and his children, and recounts the stories of Procris, Cephalus, Orithyia, Boreas, and Eumolpus. Erechtheus inherited the kingdom, while his brother Butes received the priesthoods of Athena and Poseidon Erechtheus. Eumolpus supported the Eleusinians in their war against the Athenians, and an oracle required Erechtheus to sacrifice one of his daughters for victory. After the sacrifice and the ensuing battle, Erechtheus killed Eumolpus, but Poseidon killed Erechtheus and destroyed his household.

l: Pandion, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: When Pandion died, his sons divided his inheritance: Erechtheus received the kingdom and Butes received the priesthoods of Athena and Poseidon Erechtheus. A later Pandion, identified as the son of Cecrops and Metiadusa, succeeded to the kingdom after Cecrops.

l: Erechtheus, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Erechtheus received the kingdom after Pandion’s death. He married Praxithea and had sons named Cecrops, Pandorus, and Metion and daughters named Procris, Creusa, Chthonia, and Orithyia. During the war with the Eleusinians, he sacrificed his youngest daughter as required by an oracle, killed Eumolpus in the ensuing battle, and was then killed by Poseidon, who also destroyed his household.

l: Procris, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Procris married Cephalus. After being bribed with a golden crown, she slept with Pteleon and fled to Minos when Cephalus discovered her; she later returned to Athens and reconciled with Cephalus. While hunting, she was unknowingly killed by Cephalus with a dart, and Cephalus was condemned to perpetual banishment.

l: Orithyia, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Orithyia was a daughter of Erechtheus and was carried off by Boreas while she was playing by the Ilissus. She bore Boreas the daughters Cleopatra and Chione and the winged sons Zetes and Calais.

l: Boreas, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Boreas carried off Orithyia while she was playing by the Ilissus and had intercourse with her. Their children were Cleopatra, Chione, Zetes, and Calais.

l: Cephalus, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Cephalus married Procris and later discovered her affair with Pteleon, causing her to flee to Minos. After reconciling with Procris, he accidentally killed her with a dart while hunting and was condemned to perpetual banishment.

l: Minos, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Minos fell in love with Procris and tried to seduce her. Because Pasiphae had bewitched him, women who slept with him were attacked by wild beasts, but Procris gave him a Circaean root that prevented the harm and received from him a swift dog and a straight-flying dart.

l: Eumolpus, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Eumolpus was born to Chione and Poseidon and was raised by Benthesicyme. After being banished, he went to Tegyrius, later fled to the Eleusinians, and eventually returned to Tegyrius and succeeded to the kingdom. He fought for the Eleusinians against the Athenians and was killed by Erechtheus after Erechtheus sacrificed his youngest daughter.

l: Athenians, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: The Athenians were involved in a war against the Eleusinians. Erechtheus fought on their side against Eumolpus and the Eleusinians.

l: Eleusinians, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: The Eleusinians called on Eumolpus, who came with a large Thracian force to fight on their side against the Athenians. They were opposed by Erechtheus and the Athenians.

l: Athens, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Procris returned to Athens after fleeing from Minos and was reconciled with Cephalus there. Athens was also the city whose side Erechtheus defended in the war against the Eleusinians.

l: Eleusis, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: Eumolpus fled to Eleusis after being detected in a plot against Tegyrius and made friends with the Eleusinians there. Eleusis was consequently involved in the later war against the Athenians.

l: war between the Athenians and the Eleusinians, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: A war arose between the Athenians and the Eleusinians, who called on Eumolpus to fight for them with a large Thracian force. The conflict ended with Eumolpus killed by Erechtheus, followed by Poseidon’s destruction of Erechtheus and his household.

l: sacrifice of Erechtheus's youngest daughter, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: An oracle declared that the Athenians would win the war if Erechtheus sacrificed one of his daughters. Erechtheus sacrificed his youngest daughter, and his other daughters also killed themselves because they had agreed to die together.

l: battle between Erechtheus and Eumolpus, The Library, XV. Πανδίονος δὲ ἀποθανόντος οἱ παῖδες τὰ
s: After the sacrifice of Erechtheus’s youngest daughter and the deaths of his other daughters, the battle took place. Erechtheus killed Eumolpus, but Poseidon then killed Erechtheus and destroyed his household.

l: The Library, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The unit recounts the succession of Cecrops and Pandion, the division of power among Pandion’s sons, and Aegeus’s consultation of the oracle concerning children. It describes Aegeus’s encounter with Aethra at Troezen, the death of Androgeus, and Minos’s campaign against Athens and Megara. After famine and pestilence afflicted Athens, the Athenians agreed to send seven youths and seven maidens to the Minotaur. The unit also explains the Minotaur’s Labyrinth and Daedalus’s role in constructing it.

l: Erechtheus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Erechtheus was told by the oracle that the Athenians would win their war if he slaughtered one of his daughters. After he slaughtered his youngest daughter, the others also killed themselves, and he killed Eumolpus in the ensuing battle. Poseidon destroyed Erechtheus and his house.

l: Athenians, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Athenians were promised victory if Erechtheus sacrificed a daughter. Later, they suffered famine and pestilence during Minos’s war, sacrificed the daughters of Hyacinth, and ultimately agreed to send seven youths and seven maidens to the Minotaur.

l: oracle, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The oracle told Erechtheus that the Athenians would win if he sacrificed one of his daughters. It later told Aegeus to loosen the bulging mouth of the wineskin only after reaching the height of Athens, and told the Athenians to give Minos whatever satisfaction he chose.

l: Poseidon, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Poseidon destroyed Erechtheus and his house after Erechtheus killed Eumolpus. He also had intercourse with Aethra on the same night that Aegeus lay with her.

l: Pandion, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Pandion succeeded Cecrops as king. After being expelled by the sons of Metion, he went to Megara, married Pylia, and later became king there. His sons were Aegeus, Pallas, Nisus, and Lycus.

l: Athens, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Athens was ruled by Aegeus after the sons of Pandion expelled the Metionids and divided the government. Aegeus returned there after visiting Troezen, and Minos later attacked the city with a fleet.
